full_judgment:
8. Leave was granted to consider whether the High Court Division was justified in reassessing the evidence as to the date of demand for reconveyance within Magh 1365 BS and coming to the findings that the demand was not made within that period and that the suit was barred by limitation. 

 10. The main grievance of the appellants that the High Court Division committed an error of law in reassessing the evidence as to tender of the consideration on 28 Magh 1365 BS has little ground. The well settled principle of law that in the case of a contract for reconveyance time is of the essence of contract is not disputed before us in view of the decisions in Abdul Rahim Sardar vs. Idris Ali Bepari, 11 DLR 169 and Abdur Rahman vs. Haji Ranga Laskar. 15 DLR 274. The trial Court did not miss this principle but the lower appellate Court did. The trial Court give a finding that tender was made within Magh 1365 BS as stipulated in the agreement for reconveyance but the lower appellate Court gave no finding whether or not tender was made within the said period. On the other hand, the said court relied upon a tender allegedly made beyond the period stipulated in the agreement for reconveyance in pursuance of a salish subsequent to the said period. The High Court Division was therefore obliged to consider this vital aspect of the case and give a finding whether or not the tender was made within the period stipulated in the agreement for reconveyance. 

 "As to the power of the High Court, in exercising its jurisdiction under section 100 of the Civil Procedure Code, to disturb the finding of the first appellate Court, it is now well established. The High Court can only invoke its jurisdiction under this section, if there is an error of law, or procedure committed by the first appellate Court, and such error has affected the merit of the decision, else the finding of the fact of the first appellate Court, however wrong it might appear, cannot be interfered with, by the High Court in a second appeal. The next question is, if the High Court finds an error either of law or procedure, in the decision of the first appellate Court, which has affected the merit of the decision, how the High Court shall proceed. Section 103 of the Code lays down the procedure in such a case. This section fully empowers the High Court in a second appeal, if the evidence on the record is sufficient, to determine any issue or issues of fact necessary for the disposal of the appeal, which has not been determined by the lower appellate Court, or which has been wrongly determined, by such court by reason of any illegality, omission, error or defect such as is referred to in sub-section (1) of section 100. The function of the High Court in a second appeal is not the mere correction of error of a legal proposition, or pointing out the true procedure, but also to determine properly issues of fact after making the correct exposition of law, if such determination is essential for the disposal of the appeal. Subject to this narrow jurisdiction of interference, the finding of fact of the first appellate Court is conclusive and binding upon the High Court." 

 12. In this view of the matter we have no hesitation to hold that the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division was perfectly justified in exercising his power under section 103 and giving his decision as to the tender of the consideration and demand of reconveyance particularly when, as it appears from the judgment of the High Court Division, the learned Judge was loathe to send back the case on remand to consider this point as was prayed by the learned Counsels, more than 20 years having then elapsed since the institution of the suit. 

 13. Coming to the factual aspect of the case the learned Judge of the High Court Division has analysed the evidence threadbare and concluded: 

 "The facts that the plaintiff himself said nothing as to alleged demand for reconveyance and that evidence of his son PW 2 remained uncorroborated lead but to the one and only conclusion that the plaintiffs case as to demand for reconveyance by Magh, 1365 BS was not at all proved. The reference made by the courts below to evidence as to subsequent darbar for extension of time was not justified inasmuch as if the demand for reconveyance within the stipulated time was not proved, no amount of darbar could bring back the plaintiffs claim for reconveyance to life. Thus I am of the opinion that the plaintiffs suit was barred inasmuch as if the demand for reconveyance within the stipulated time was not proved, no amount or darbar could bring back the plaintiffs claim for reconveyance to life. Thus I am of the opinion that the plaintiffs suit was barred inasmuch as he failed to prove that the demand for reconveyance was made within the stipulated time. In such view of the matter, the suit as a whole is liable to be dismissed."
